processing: A pan-fired style green from young shoots, typically one bud with two leaves, cooled and re-moistened, rolled, then finished in a tumbling pan to lift colour and aroma.
harvest_season: Spring is the prized picking and summer tea ranks below it; southern Zhejiang starts early, often before most of the province.
appearance_dry: Fine, tight and straight strands of even size, with a glossy deep green colour.
appearance_liquor: Clear and bright, a fresh yellow-green.
appearance_wet: Tender, even shoots of a yellow-green colour.
taste_profile: A clean, lasting green fragrance over a full, mellow body with a sweet finish, and its reputation rests on staying fragrant into the third cup.

brewing.notes: Brew it in a glass or a porcelain cup. It is a sturdier leaf than a bud-only green, so three infusions are realistic; the third is the one the name promises.

vintage_note: As usual for Zhejiang greens, it is sold as the current year's spring tea and is best drunk within the year. The earliest lots reach the market ahead of most Zhejiang teas and cost more. It is not a tea to age.
description:
Sanbeixiang, literally 'three cups of fragrance', is the county green of Taishun in the far south of Zhejiang, close to the Fujian border. The name is the selling point: the aroma is meant to survive three infusions, where many delicate greens are spent after two.

It is picked to a one-bud, two-leaf standard, so there is more leaf in it than in the bud-only teas of the region. That gives it the firmer, more mellow body it is known for, with a sweetness at the end rather than just a light floral lift.

Expect a clear, bright cup and a clean green fragrance. As with other Zhejiang greens, water well off the boil and a roomy vessel keep it from stewing. If it turns bitter, the fix is usually a cooler pour or less leaf.

It is bought as a seasonal spring tea, and the name is a protected regional mark. Ask for the harvest date and treat a label reading only 'three cups' with some care, since the phrase alone says little about where the leaf grew.
history:
A travel account citing the county gazetteer traces written mention of tea in Taishun to 1633, in the late Ming, though that refers to local tea generally. Sanbeixiang had its strongest reputation in the 1950s and 1960s, then lost ground in the late 1990s when many producers worked to their own standards and the name's credibility suffered.

The revival came through protection: the name was registered as a geographical indication trademark in 2009, and the agriculture ministry gave it agricultural geographical indication status in 2010. It joined China's national catalogue of agricultural brands in 2019.
